# Why hearts are missed

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-cross-checked' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D0 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- State how common congenital heart disease is and how much of it is found before birth.
- Name the two failures that one study of missed diagnoses found most often.
- Explain why the four-chamber view alone is not enough.
- List the features of a screening service that detects more.

## The size of the gap

Congenital heart disease affects about 8 in every 1000 live births and is a leading cause of illness and death in infancy. [1]

Detection before birth varies widely between regions and between lesions. Overall, fewer than half of cardiac anomalies are identified before birth. [2]


## You cannot screen by risk factor

A high proportion of the heart disease that could be detected before birth occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor and no extracardiac anomaly. This is why a quality routine screen of every pregnancy, and timely referral, matter. [3]


## Where the miss happens

In one retrospective study of missed diagnoses, views that did not meet technical criteria contributed to about half of the misses. In nearly a third, the view was technically adequate but the abnormal anatomy was not recognised. [4]

These are two different failures. This course practises both skills: obtaining every plane to a standard, and knowing what each normal plane looks like.


## Why detection varies

Part of the variation is explained by the examiner's ability, transducer frequency, maternal body habitus, abdominal scars, gestational age, amniotic fluid volume and fetal position. [5]

When the fetus is lying unfavourably, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed. [6]


## Four chambers are not enough

The four-chamber and three-vessel views need much more than a count of structures. [7]

Some lesions, such as transposition of the great arteries and coarctation of the aorta, may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone. Some lesions are not discovered until later in pregnancy. [8]

Adding the outflow-tract and great-vessel views raises detection of major malformations above the four-chamber view alone. It allows detection of tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, double-outlet right ventricle and truncus arteriosus. [9, 10]

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can all have a four-chamber view that looks normal. They are typically abnormal in the three-vessel view. [11]

The same standard sweep can also pick up aortic and pulmonary valve stenosis, which may become more severe as pregnancy advances. [12]


## What a good screening service does

Four things can improve the performance of a screening programme: continuous training based on feedback, a low threshold for referral for echocardiography, standardised protocols and easy access to fetal heart specialists. [13]

Each practice is encouraged to audit its stored images or clips against set quality criteria, to review its own detection rates and diagnostic accuracy every year, and to provide further training where needed. [14]


## What this course asks of you

Learn one sweep and do it the same way on every patient. Learn the criteria for each plane. Use the clip drills to practise telling, quickly, whether a plane meets them. The few-second limit in the drills is a training exercise, not a clinical standard.

Keep two situations apart. A view that could not be obtained is an incomplete examination: with an unfavourable lie, more time or a second examination may be needed. A view that looks abnormal is a suspected abnormality, and that fetus is a candidate for fetal echocardiography. [6, 15]

## Habits that close the gap

- [ ] Routine second-trimester screen includes situs, four-chamber, outflow-tract and great-vessel views [16, 17]
- [ ] Four-chamber and three-vessel views judged against their criteria, not by counting structures [7]
- [ ] A normal four-chamber view is never taken as proof of a normal heart [8, 11]
- [ ] Suspected abnormality: fetus is a candidate for fetal echocardiography [15]
- [ ] View not obtained: more time or a second examination [6]
- [ ] Stored images audited against criteria set in advance [14]
- [ ] Detection rates and diagnostic accuracy reviewed every year [14]

## Still to be written

- Detection rates in India and by lesion type - needs an Indian source.
- Outcome benefit of prenatal diagnosis for specific lesions (why detection matters for the baby) - needs a source beyond this guideline.

# The normal heart in five views

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-cross-checked' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D1 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.4

## You will be able to

- Perform the five-plane sweep in order and say what each plane must show.
- Set up the machine for a cardiac screen.
- Give the normal values for heart size, axis and rate, and the rates that need referral.
- List the criteria that make a four-chamber view normal.
- Confirm normal outflow tracts and a normal three-vessel-and-trachea view.

## Why five views

A screening scan does not need to name the lesion. This unit teaches one systematic assessment of five views, done in the same order every time.

Congenital heart disease affects about 8 in every 1000 live births, and fewer than half of cardiac anomalies are found before birth. [1, 2]

Most detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor at all. That is why the routine scan matters more than the referral list. [3]

Some lesions, such as transposition and coarctation, may show nothing in the four-chamber plane. Adding the outflow-tract and great-vessel views raises detection above the four-chamber view alone. [4, 5, 6]

The examination should include situs, the four-chamber view, and the outflow-tract and great-vessel views, ideally between 18 and 22 weeks. [7, 8]


## Set up before you scan

Use the highest transducer frequency that still penetrates. Harmonic imaging helps when the abdominal wall is thick and in the third trimester. [9, 10]

Choose the cardiac preset: high frame rate, more contrast, low persistence, a single focal zone and a narrow sector. [11]

Zoom until the heart fills at least a third to a half of the screen. Use cine-loop to watch the valves through the whole cycle. [12, 13]

Store stills and clips of each view so the examination can be reviewed later. [14]


## The sweep

The examination is one continuous transverse sweep towards the fetal head through five planes: upper abdomen, four-chamber view, left ventricular outflow tract, right ventricular outflow tract with the three-vessel view, and the three-vessel-and-trachea view. [15, 16, 17]

The upper planes are a continuum, not fixed pictures. They are likely to be judged more reliably live or on a clip than from stills alone. [18]

If the fetus is lying badly, more examination time or a second examination may be needed. [19]


## Plane I: left, right and situs

First work out which side of the fetus is left and which is right from its position in the uterus. Only then confirm that stomach and heart are both on the left. [20]

At the level of the abdominal circumference: stomach on the left, descending aorta to the left of the spine, inferior vena cava to the right. [21]

Normal abdominal situs stands in for normal atrial arrangement. If heart or stomach is not on the left, suspect a situs abnormality. [22, 23]


## Plane II: size, position, axis, rate

A normal heart is usually no larger than a third of the chest area. [24]

It lies mainly in the left chest with its axis pointing left at about 45 degrees, 20 degrees either way. You can judge axis and position even when the rest of the view is poor. [25, 26]

An abnormal axis raises the chance of a heart defect, especially of the outflow tracts. A heart that is pushed out of place points to something beside it: diaphragmatic hernia, a lung mass, or a small or absent lung. [27, 28]

Rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute and regular. Skipped (ectopic) beats are the most common rhythm disturbance and are often benign; in low-risk populations they are not linked to a higher risk of structural heart disease. Further assessment is indicated when they come more often than every three to five beats, or when the rhythm stays irregular for more than 1 to 2 weeks. [29, 30, 31]

A brief slow rate, associated with probe pressure, is seen in normal second-trimester fetuses. A rate that stays at 110 or below in a well fetus, or at 180 or above, needs specialist assessment. [32, 33]


## Plane II: the four-chamber criteria

Seeing four chambers is not the same as a normal four-chamber view. The view is judged against specific criteria. [34]

Atria: similar in size, foramen ovale flap moving in the left atrium, septum primum present. Where you can, show at least one pulmonary vein entering the left atrium. [35, 36]

Ventricles: similar in size, walls not thick. The moderator band marks the right ventricle; the smooth left ventricle forms the apex. [37, 38]

One ventricle clearly smaller than the other in mid-pregnancy is not a variant. Think of coarctation, an evolving hypoplastic left heart, and anomalous pulmonary veins. [38]

Septum: follow it from apex to crux. It is best seen with the beam at right angles; with the beam along the septum, drop-out can fake a defect near the crux. [39, 40]

Valves: two, opening separately and freely, with the tricuspid attached slightly nearer the apex than the mitral. Abnormal alignment of the two valves can be a key finding in anomalies such as atrioventricular septal defect. [41]

A thin rim of pericardial fluid, up to 2 mm, is normal. [42]


## Plane III: left ventricular outflow tract

A vessel leaves the left ventricle. Its front wall runs straight on from the ventricular septum, and it does not divide. The valve is thin and opens freely. [43, 44, 45]

This view shows outlet septal defects and conotruncal and aortic valve problems that the four-chamber view hides. [46]


## Plane IV: right ventricular outflow tract and three vessels

A vessel leaves the right ventricle, crosses in front of the aorta almost at a right angle, and divides after a short course. It is usually slightly larger than the aorta. Its valve is thin and opens freely. [43, 47, 48]

At the least, the two great arteries should be about the same size. A clear difference needs further assessment. [49]

Three vessels in a line: pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava, from left to right and from front to back, each smaller than the one before. Check number, size, alignment and arrangement. [50]

Transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a septal defect can all pass the four-chamber view. They typically fail this one. [51]


## Plane V: three vessels and trachea

The ductal arch and the aortic arch both pass to the left of the trachea and meet in a V. The two arches are similar in size. The trachea is a bright ring around a small dark centre. [52, 53, 54]

This is the view for the arch: coarctation, right arch, double arch, vascular rings and an aberrant right subclavian artery. [55, 56]


## Colour Doppler

Colour is not mandatory for screening but is encouraged once you are competent with it. [57]

Keep the colour box small and over the area of interest. Set the scale to about 50 to 70 cm/s for the heart and arteries, and about 15 to 25 cm/s for veins. [58, 59]

Normal colour shows forward flow through all four valves and both arches. It makes the V easier to see and exposes leaking valves and reversed flow in an arch. [60]


## When the screen is not normal

Any fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening should have a fetal echocardiogram. [61]

About half of missed diagnoses in one study came from views that did not meet technical standards, and nearly a third from not recognising the abnormality on an adequate view. Both are trainable. [62]

# Setting up the machine for the heart

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D2 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.3

## You will be able to

- Choose the gestation, probe and frequency for a cardiac screen.
- Set the image for the heart: frame rate, persistence, focus, sector and zoom.
- Set colour for a second-trimester screen.
- Apply the safety principle for output and exposure.
- Say what to do when the fetus is lying badly.

## When to scan

The cardiac screening examination is performed optimally between 18 and 22 weeks. [1]

A screen at 20 to 22 weeks is less likely to need a second scan to complete it than one at 18 to 20 weeks, although many patients prefer to know about major defects as early as possible. [2]

Many anatomical structures can still be seen satisfactorily beyond 22 weeks. [3]


## Probe and frequency

Use the highest transducer frequency you can, accepting the trade-off between resolution and penetration. [4]

The echocardiography guideline prefers curvilinear transducers and recommends a range of 2 to 7 MHz for the late second and third trimesters. Linear and sector transducers may also be used. [5]

Tissue harmonic imaging improves the image, especially when the abdominal wall is thick and in the third trimester. [6]


## The cardiac image

Settings should favour a high frame rate with increased contrast and high resolution. That means low persistence, a single focal zone and a relatively narrow image field. Cardiac presets usually have these built in. [7]

For fetal echocardiography, frame rates above 30 to 40 Hz are recommended. Narrowing the sector and choosing an appropriate depth help to achieve them. [8]

The screening settings at a glance. [7, 9]

| Setting | For the heart |
|---|---|
| Frame rate | High |
| Persistence | Low |
| Focal zones | One |
| Image field (sector) | Relatively narrow |
| Contrast and resolution | Increased contrast, high resolution |
| Magnification | Heart fills at least a third to a half of the screen |


## Zoom and cine-loop

Magnify the image until the heart fills at least one third to one half of the screen. [9]

Use cine-loop to help the real-time assessment, for example to confirm that the valve leaflets move through the whole cardiac cycle. [10]


## Colour, when you use it

Keep the colour box narrow and only over the area of interest. This preserves frame rate and the quality of the colour image. [11]

For a second-trimester screen, set the velocity scale to about 50 to 70 cm/s for the heart and arteries and about 15 to 25 cm/s for veins. Low colour persistence is ordinarily built into cardiac presets. [12]

Unit D7 covers colour in full.


## Safety

Fetal echocardiography follows the principle of keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable. Operators should be aware of the thermal and mechanical indices and limit power output and exposure time. [13]

At an early cardiac screen with Doppler, the thermal index should be 1.0 or less and exposure as short as possible. [14]


## Store what you see

Archive still frames and clips of the recommended structures and views so that the examination can be reviewed later for adequacy, labelling laterality and orientation where appropriate. [15]


## When the view is poor

Several things affect what can be seen: transducer frequency, maternal body habitus, abdominal scars, gestational age, amniotic fluid volume and fetal position, as well as the examiner's ability. [16]

When the fetal lie is unfavourable, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed. [17]

In a fetal echocardiogram, if diagnostic images cannot be obtained after optimisation, the report should state the limitation. [18]

## Before the sweep

- [ ] Highest frequency that still penetrates; harmonics on if the wall is thick or the pregnancy is late [4, 6]
- [ ] High frame rate, low persistence, single focal zone, relatively narrow field (usually the cardiac preset) [7]
- [ ] Heart magnified to at least a third to a half of the screen [9]
- [ ] Cine-loop used to review valve movement [10]
- [ ] If colour is used: narrow box; scale about 50 to 70 cm/s for heart and arteries, about 15 to 25 cm/s for veins (second trimester) [11, 12]
- [ ] Stills and clips of the recommended views stored [15]
- [ ] Unfavourable lie: more time or a second examination [17]

## Still to be written

- Voluson-specific steps: which preset, where each control is, recommended values on this machine - needs the machine manual and the editor's own settings.
- Depth, gain and dynamic range advice in practical terms - needs a source.
- Techniques for the difficult patient (high BMI, anterior spine, late gestation) - planned for D14; needs a source.
- How frame rate, sector width and depth trade off physically - planned for XA4; needs a physics source.

# Laterality and situs

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D3 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- Establish fetal left and right before judging any organ's position.
- State what the upper-abdomen plane shows in normal situs.
- Explain why normal abdominal situs stands in for normal atrial arrangement.
- Recognise when to suspect a situs abnormality, and tell it from a heart that has been displaced.

## Left and right come first

To assess situs, first determine fetal laterality: which side is the fetal right and which the fetal left, from the position of the fetus in the uterus. Only then confirm that the stomach and the heart are both on the fetal left. [1]

The order matters. If you decide that the stomach is 'on the left' because that is where the stomach usually is, you have assumed the answer.


## The upper-abdomen plane

A transverse sweep, moving the transducer towards the fetal head from the abdomen to the chest, shows the abdominal situs first and then the four-chamber view. [2]

Abdominal situs is assessed at the level of the standard abdominal circumference. Normal: stomach on the left, descending aorta to the left of the spine, inferior vena cava to the right of the spine. [3]

| Structure | Normal position in the upper-abdomen plane |
|---|---|
| Stomach | Fetal left |
| Descending aorta | Left of the spine |
| Inferior vena cava | Right of the spine |


## What normal abdominal situs tells you

Normal abdominal situs is a surrogate for normal atrial situs: right atrium on the right, left atrium on the left. [4]


## Then the heart

The heart lies mainly in the left chest, with its long axis pointing to the left at about 45 degrees, plus or minus 20 degrees, relative to the front-to-back axis of the chest. [5]

Position and axis can be judged even when the four-chamber view itself is not seen well. [6]


## When something is not on the left

Suspect a situs abnormality when the heart, the stomach, or both are not on the left. [7]

A fetus with a suspected abnormality on cardiac screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography. [8]


## A displaced heart is a different problem

A heart can be pushed or pulled out of its normal position by something next to it: a diaphragmatic hernia, a space-occupying lesion such as a congenital pulmonary airway malformation, or a lung that is small or absent. A leftward shift of the axis may also occur with gastroschisis and omphalocele. [9]

An abnormal cardiac axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly. [10]


## What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

To assign abdominal situs, the examiner evaluates an upper abdominal cross-section showing the stomach, the liver, the descending aorta and the systemic veins, with careful attention to fetal lie and transducer orientation. [11]

Two-dimensional imaging is required for visceral and atrial situs; colour Doppler is optional for it. [12]

A sagittal view of the two venae cavae establishes whether the inferior vena cava is continuous and whether both venae cavae lie on the same side. [13, 14]


## Record it

Stored images should carry labels for laterality and orientation where appropriate. [15]

## Plane I checklist

- [ ] Fetal left and right established from the position of the fetus [1]
- [ ] Stomach on the fetal left [3]
- [ ] Descending aorta left of the spine; inferior vena cava right of the spine [3]
- [ ] Heart mainly in the left chest; axis about 45 degrees to the left (plus or minus 20) [5]
- [ ] Heart or stomach not on the left: situs abnormality suspected [7]
- [ ] Laterality and orientation labelled on stored images where appropriate [15]

## Still to be written

- Named practical methods for working out fetal left and right (for example from presentation and spine position) - not described in the guidelines held; needs a source or the editor's own teaching method.
- The patterns of abnormal situs (situs inversus, right and left isomerism) and what each looks like in the abdomen plane - planned for the lesion atlas; needs a source.
- Terms for heart position (dextrocardia, mesocardia, dextroposition) and how to use them in a report - needs a source.
- How often abnormal situs carries heart disease - needs a source.

# The four-chamber view in depth

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D4 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- Judge heart size, position and axis.
- Apply the criteria for the atria, pulmonary veins, ventricles, septum and atrioventricular valves.
- Avoid the common false alarms: a pericardial rim and septal drop-out.
- Say what a normal four-chamber view does not exclude.

## More than a count

The four-chamber view requires much more than counting four chambers. [1]

Work through it in the same order every time: size, position and axis, then atria, veins, ventricles, septum, valves.


## Size and the rim of fluid

A normal heart is usually no larger than one third of the area of the chest. [2]

A small amount of pericardial fluid, 2 mm or less in thickness at end-systole, is common in the second and third trimesters and is normal. A thin dark rim around the heart should not be mistaken for an effusion. [3]


## Position and axis

The heart lies mainly in the left chest. Its long axis normally points to the left at about 45 degrees, plus or minus 20 degrees, relative to the front-to-back axis of the chest. [4]

An abnormal axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly. [5]

A heart displaced from its normal position may point to a diaphragmatic hernia, a space-occupying lesion in the chest, or a small or absent lung. [6]


## Atria

The two atria normally look similar in size. The flap of the foramen ovale moves within the left atrium. The septum primum, the lower rim of the atrial septum, should be present. [7]

The crux of the heart is the point where the lower atrial septum meets the upper ventricular septum and where the atrioventricular valves insert. [8]


## Pulmonary veins

Where technically feasible, at least one pulmonary vein should be seen entering the left atrium on grey-scale. Colour can help but is not mandatory for this. [9]

If colour is used to show the veins, display it alongside the grey-scale image to help avoid false-negative findings. [10]


## Ventricles

The moderator band near the apex identifies the morphological right ventricle. The left ventricular apex looks smooth and forms the apex of the heart. [11]

The ventricles should look similar in size, with no thickening of the walls. [12]

Mild disproportion can be a normal variant in the third trimester. Right-left asymmetry in mid-gestation is different: it warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return. [12]


## Ventricular septum

Examine the septum from apex to crux and, if possible, sweep from its most posterior part towards the outflow tracts. [13]

The septum is seen best with the beam perpendicular to it. With the beam parallel to the septum, acoustic drop-out can falsely suggest a defect near the crux. [14]

Small septal defects of 1 to 2 mm can be very difficult to confirm, particularly when fetal size and position are unfavourable. Most are of limited clinical significance and may close on their own before birth. [15, 16]


## Atrioventricular valves

There should be two separate atrioventricular valves that open separately and freely. The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve inserts closer to the apex than the mitral valve: the normal offset. [17]

Abnormal alignment of the two valves can be a key finding in anomalies such as atrioventricular septal defect. [17]


## Rate and rhythm

Normal rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute, with a regular rhythm. [18]

Unit D8 covers rate and rhythm in full.


## What a normal four-chamber view does not exclude

Some lesions, for example transposition of the great arteries and coarctation of the aorta, may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone. [19]

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can have a four-chamber view that looks normal. [20]


## What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

The fetal heart should be examined from at least two orthogonal planes, depending on the size, thickness and orientation of the structure. [21]

The cardiac axis must be assessed; measuring the angle is optional. A complete study requires a measured ratio of cardiac to thoracic area. [22, 23]

Pulmonary venous connections must be shown from at least one vein on each side, with two-dimensional and colour imaging. [24]

Both two-dimensional and colour images are required to assess the ventricular septum and to locate any defect. [25]

## Four-chamber view checklist

- [ ] Heart usually no larger than a third of the chest area [2]
- [ ] Mainly in the left chest; axis about 45 degrees to the left (plus or minus 20) [4]
- [ ] Rate 120 to 160 per minute, regular [18]
- [ ] Atria similar in size; foramen ovale flap moving in the left atrium; septum primum present [7]
- [ ] At least one pulmonary vein entering the left atrium, where technically feasible [9]
- [ ] Ventricles similar in size; walls not thick; moderator band near the apex of the right ventricle [11, 12]
- [ ] Septum examined from apex to crux, beam perpendicular where possible [13, 14]
- [ ] Two atrioventricular valves opening separately and freely; normal offset [17]
- [ ] Pericardial fluid no more than a thin rim (2 mm or less) [3]

# Outflow tracts

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-cross-checked' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D5 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- Obtain both outflow-tract views by the sweep or the rotational technique.
- Confirm the three things that make the outflow tracts normal.
- Identify the aorta and the pulmonary artery by their features.
- Name the lesions that outflow-tract views reveal.

## Why these views are not optional

The left and right outflow-tract views, with the three-vessel and three-vessel-and-trachea views, are an integral part of the cardiac screening examination. [1]

Including outflow-tract and great-vessel views raises detection of major malformations above the four-chamber view alone. It allows detection of tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, double-outlet right ventricle and truncus arteriosus. [2]

The same views can identify aortic and pulmonary valve stenosis, which may become more severe as pregnancy advances. [3]

In a survey of more than 18 000 fetuses, 93% of examinations with an adequate four-chamber view also achieved a satisfactory outflow-tract evaluation. [4]


## What to establish

For the two great arteries, establish four things: each is connected to the correct ventricle; their size; their position relative to each other; and that the semilunar valves look normal and open normally. [5]

Alongside those four checks, three features of continuity and crossing are confirmed; they do not replace the four. The vessel leaving the left ventricle has its anterior wall continuous with the ventricular septum and does not divide: the aorta. The vessel leaving the right ventricle divides: the pulmonary artery. The two great arteries cross each other. [6, 7, 8]

| Feature | Aorta | Pulmonary artery |
|---|---|---|
| Arises from | Left ventricle | Right ventricle |
| Divides early | No | Yes, after a short course |
| Wall continuity | Anterior wall continuous with the ventricular septum | - |
| Relative size | Usually slightly smaller | Usually slightly larger |
| Course, each relative to the other | The ascending aorta is the more posterior | Runs to the left of the ascending aorta and crosses it at almost a right angle |


## Two ways to get there

Sweep technique: from the four-chamber view, sweep transversely towards the fetal head. The left outflow, the right outflow, the three-vessel view and the three-vessel-and-trachea view appear in sequence. [9]

Rotational technique: from the four-chamber view, rotate the transducer towards the fetal right shoulder. It is easier when the septum is perpendicular to the beam and may need slightly more skill. It optimises the left outflow tract, especially the outlet septum in continuity with the anterior wall of the aorta. [10]

Once the left outflow tract is obtained, angle towards the head until the pulmonary artery is seen running almost at right angles to the aorta. The relation of the two outflow tracts is shown best on cine clips, not stills. [11]

When the fetal lie is unfavourable, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed. [12]


## Left ventricular outflow tract

The view confirms a great vessel arising from the morphological left ventricle. Document the continuity between the ventricular septum and the anterior wall of the vessel. [13]

Strictly, only the head and neck vessels arising from it confirm that the vessel is the aorta. [13]

The aortic valve should move freely and should not be thickened. [14]

This view helps to identify outlet ventricular septal defects, conotruncal abnormalities and aortic valve abnormalities that are not visible in the four-chamber view. [15]


## Right ventricular outflow tract

The view confirms the pulmonary artery arising from the morphological right ventricle and branching after a short course. The pulmonary valve should move freely and should not be thickened. [7]

The normal pulmonary artery runs to the left of the more posterior ascending aorta, is usually slightly larger than the ascending aorta in fetal life, and crosses it at almost a right angle. [8]


## Size

At the least, show that the two great arteries are approximately equal in size. A major discrepancy should lead to further evaluation. [16]


## What is not part of the screen

Sagittal views of the aortic and ductal arches, and assessment of the neck vessels, are not currently part of the routine cardiac screening examination. [17]


## What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

The normal left outflow view shows the outflow below the aortic valve, the valve, the region above it and the ascending aorta. [18]

The normal right outflow view shows the tract below the pulmonary valve, the valve and the proximal pulmonary trunk; the bifurcation may come into the plane. [19]

The origins of the right and left pulmonary arteries need two-dimensional and colour imaging; measuring them is optional. [20]

## Outflow tracts checklist

- [ ] Vessel from the left ventricle; anterior wall continuous with the septum; does not divide [6, 13]
- [ ] Aortic valve moving freely, not thickened [14]
- [ ] Vessel from the right ventricle; divides after a short course [6, 7]
- [ ] Pulmonary valve moving freely, not thickened [7]
- [ ] The two great arteries cross [6]
- [ ] Great arteries approximately equal in size [16]
- [ ] Clip of the outflow tracts stored [11, 21]

# Three-vessel and three-vessel-and-trachea views

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D6 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.3

## You will be able to

- Assess the three-vessel view for number, size, alignment and arrangement.
- Describe the normal three-vessel-and-trachea view: the V, its side, and the trachea.
- Name the lesions these two views help to detect.
- Explain how a finding here changes what happens next.

## A continuum, not two pictures

The axial appearances of the right outflow tract, the branch pulmonary arteries and the ductal and aortic arches form a continuum of views. What you see varies with the orientation of the transducer and the lie of the fetus. [1]

Assessment is likely to be more reliable live or on cine-loop than from still images alone. [1]


## The three-vessel view

Assess four things: the number of vessels, their size, their alignment and their arrangement. [2]

From left to right the vessels are the pulmonary artery, the aorta and the right superior vena cava. The pulmonary artery is the most anterior and the vena cava the most posterior. The diameters decrease from left to right. [2]

| Vessel | Side | Front to back | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pulmonary artery | Left | Most anterior | Largest |
| Aorta | Middle | Middle | Middle |
| Superior vena cava | Right | Most posterior | Smallest |

The pulmonary artery is usually slightly larger than the ascending aorta in fetal life. The superior vena cava lies to the right of the aorta. [3]


## The three-vessel-and-trachea view

This is a slightly oblique transverse plane, towards the head from the three-vessel view. It shows the main pulmonary artery continuing into the ductus arteriosus, with the transverse aortic arch just to its right. [4]

The trachea appears as a bright ring around a small fluid-filled space. [4]

Normally the ductus arteriosus and the aortic arch both run to the left of the trachea and meet at an acute angle, forming a V. The right superior vena cava and the thymus are also seen in this plane. [5]

The screening checklist asks for two things here: the V-sign, with both arches to the left of the trachea, and ductal and aortic arches of similar size. [6]

The thymus appears as a relatively dark area between the great vessels and the front of the chest. [7]

The aortic arch lies slightly nearer the head than the ductal arch, so showing both together may need a small adjustment away from a true axial plane. [8]


## Adding colour

Colour helps to show the V-sign and can highlight reversed flow in the ductus arteriosus or the aortic arch. [9]


## What these views detect

The two views help to detect anomalies of the outflow tracts, the aortic arch and the systemic veins, including a persistent left superior vena cava, and anomalies of the thymus. [10]

The three-vessel-and-trachea view is particularly useful for abnormalities of the aortic arch such as coarctation, vascular rings and an aberrant right subclavian artery. It is likely to enable detection of coarctation, right aortic arch and double aortic arch. [11, 12]

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can have a four-chamber view that looks normal. They are typically abnormal in the three-vessel view. [13]

| Check | Normal | Question to ask if not |
|---|---|---|
| Number | Three vessels | Is there a fourth vessel, or only two? |
| Size | Decreasing from left to right; arches similar in size | Is one great artery or one arch much smaller? |
| Alignment and arrangement | Pulmonary artery, aorta, vena cava in a line from left-front to right-back | Is the order or the line wrong? |
| Side of the arches | Both left of the trachea, meeting in a V | Does an arch pass to the right of the trachea, or on both sides? |


## Why a finding here matters

Anomalies found on the three-vessel views can change counselling and management. What follows depends on the anomaly found; none of these follows from every abnormal view. The guideline's examples: testing for 22q11 microdeletion; planning where delivery takes place, as in complete transposition; being ready to give prostaglandin; being ready for airway problems from vascular compression. [14]

A fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography. [15]


## What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

In the three-vessel view, abnormalities of vessel number, size, alignment or arrangement should be recorded. [16]

In the normal three-vessel-and-trachea view the two arches join the descending aorta on the left of the trachea. Colour Doppler should demonstrate patency and direction of flow in both arches. [17, 18]

Aortic and ductal arch sidedness should be documented at every fetal echocardiogram. [19]

Colour and power Doppler in the three-vessel-and-trachea view can help to identify an aberrant subclavian artery. [20]

## Three-vessel views checklist

- [ ] Three vessels: pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava, from left to right [2]
- [ ] Sizes decrease from left to right [2]
- [ ] Vessels in line, pulmonary artery most anterior, vena cava most posterior [2]
- [ ] Three-vessel-and-trachea view: ductal and aortic arches meet in a V [5]
- [ ] Both arches to the left of the trachea [5, 6]
- [ ] Arches similar in size [6]
- [ ] Clip of these views stored [1, 21]

## Still to be written

- What each abnormal pattern looks like (four vessels with a left superior vena cava, U-shaped ring of a right arch with left duct, small aortic arch of coarctation) - the table above only poses the questions; the answers need a source and belong to the lesion atlas.
- Normal size ratios of the vessels and arches by gestation - planned for XA6; needs a source.
- How to recognise a small or absent thymus - needs a source.
- The third table column ('question to ask if not') is the drafter's wording of the four checks, not a guideline statement - the editor to confirm or replace.

# Colour Doppler in screening

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-cross-checked' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D7 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.1

## You will be able to

- Say whether colour Doppler is required for cardiac screening.
- Set the colour box, velocity scale and persistence for the heart and for veins.
- Describe normal colour flow through the heart and the great arteries.
- Name the abnormal patterns colour makes easier to see.
- Apply the safety limits for Doppler in early pregnancy.

## Is colour required?

Colour flow Doppler is not mandatory in cardiac screening. The 2023 guideline encourages examiners to become familiar with it and to add it to the routine scan, and it can be used when the operator feels competent. [1, 2]

Colour may be valuable in obese patients and may further improve detection of major heart disease in low-risk pregnancies. [3]

This unit treats colour as an addition to the grey-scale screen taught in unit D1.


## What normal colour shows

In a normal heart, colour shows forward flow across both atrioventricular valves, both semilunar valves and both great arteries. [4]

In the three-vessel-and-trachea view, colour helps to show the V formed by the two arches. [4]

A pulmonary vein entering the left atrium should be shown on grey-scale where technically feasible. Colour can help with this but is not mandatory for it. [5]


## What colour exposes

Colour highlights abnormal flow patterns such as regurgitation through an atrioventricular valve and reversed flow in the ductus arteriosus or the aortic arch. [4]

In a full fetal echocardiogram, colour is used to look for valve stenosis and regurgitation, flow across the foramen ovale, the integrity of the septa and the patency of vessels. [6]


## Setting up colour

Keep the colour box narrow and place it only over the area of interest. This preserves frame rate and the quality of the colour image. [7]

For a second-trimester screen, set the colour velocity scale to about 50 to 70 cm/s for the heart and the arteries. Use a lower scale, about 15 to 25 cm/s, for veins. Low colour persistence is ordinarily built into cardiac presets. [8]

For a full fetal echocardiogram, the echocardiography guideline says to set the scale to suit the velocities of interest, and to adjust colour gain and persistence so that colour fills the chamber or vessel without hiding the grey-scale image. [9]

Starting settings for a second-trimester screen. [7, 8]

| Looking at | Colour velocity scale | Other settings |
|---|---|---|
| Valves, ventricles, great arteries, arches | About 50 to 70 cm/s | Narrow box; low persistence (ordinarily in the cardiac preset) |
| Veins, such as the pulmonary veins | About 15 to 25 cm/s | Narrow box |


## Colour beside grey-scale

When you use colour to show the pulmonary veins entering the left atrium, display it alongside the grey-scale image. This helps to avoid false-negative findings. [10]


## Power Doppler

The echocardiography guideline describes power Doppler as showing the strength of the Doppler signal, not the frequency shift. In fetal echocardiography it helps to show small vessels, slow flow such as in veins, and septal defects. Directional power Doppler adds the direction of flow. [11]


## Colour in early pregnancy

For early cardiac screening, colour Doppler, or high-quality power Doppler with bidirectional flow mapping, or both, are recommended in addition to grey-scale. [12]

In early screening, use Doppler mainly for the four-chamber view and the three-vessel-and-trachea view. Keep the thermal index at 1.0 or less and the exposure as short as possible, usually no more than 5 to 10 minutes. [13]

At the early scan, the balance between colour and grey-scale is adjusted to favour the flow signal in the small cardiac structures. [14]

For early fetal echocardiography, which is a different examination, the echocardiography guideline says to keep the thermal and mechanical indices at or below 1.0 and to use Doppler sparingly. [15]

## When colour is used on a second-trimester screen

- [ ] Colour box narrow, over the area of interest only [7]
- [ ] Scale about 50 to 70 cm/s for heart and arteries; about 15 to 25 cm/s for veins [8]
- [ ] Pulmonary veins: colour shown beside the grey-scale image [10]
- [ ] Colour can show forward flow across all four valves and both great arteries [4]
- [ ] Colour can help to show the V of the two arches at the three-vessel-and-trachea view [4]
- [ ] At an early screen instead: thermal index 1.0 or less, Doppler exposure kept short [13]

## Still to be written

- Common colour traps (aliasing, colour bleeding over a septum, wrong scale hiding a jet) with how to recognise each - needs a source; partly planned for D10 and XA4.
- How to use colour on the ventricular septum to look for a defect at screening level - not stated in the screening guideline.
- Voluson-specific colour presets and HD-flow - needs a source and the editor's input.

# Rate and rhythm for the screener

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-cross-checked' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D8 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.1

## You will be able to

- Give the normal fetal heart rate at screening.
- State when ectopic beats or an irregular rhythm need further assessment.
- Tell transient slowing from persistent bradycardia, and transient speeding from persistent tachycardia.
- Name the rhythm findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography.
- Describe in outline how a specialist works out the mechanism of an arrhythmia.

## Normal

The normal heart rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute, and the rhythm should be regular. [1]

The screener's task is not to name the arrhythmia. It is to recognise the findings that the guideline lists as needing further assessment. The guideline does not give a rule for every pattern in between; see the missing claims for this unit.


## The irregular beat

Ectopic beats, seen as skipped beats, are the most common rhythm disturbance. They are often benign and resolve on their own. In low-risk populations they are not linked to a higher risk of structural heart disease. [2]

Further assessment is indicated when ectopic episodes are frequent, meaning more often than every three to five beats, or when the rhythm stays irregular for more than one to two weeks. [3]


## The slow heart

Transient bradycardia is seen in normal second-trimester fetuses and is associated with pressure from the transducer. [4]

A rate that stays at 110 beats per minute or below in a fetus that is otherwise well needs timely evaluation by a fetal cardiac specialist. Possible causes include frequent blocked atrial ectopic beats, atrioventricular block and sinus bradycardia. [4]

Recurrent decelerations of the fetal heart rate in the third trimester can reflect fetal hypoxia. [5]


## The fast heart

A mild, brief rise to 160 to 180 beats per minute can be a normal variant during fetal movement. [6]

A rate that stays at 180 beats per minute or above should be evaluated further for a tachyarrhythmia or fetal hypoxia. [6]


## At a glance

Rate and rhythm findings and what each means at screening. [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]

| Finding | Meaning for the screener |
|---|---|
| 120 to 160 per minute, regular | Normal |
| Occasional skipped beats | The most common rhythm disturbance; often benign |
| Skipped beats more often than every three to five beats, or irregular for more than one to two weeks | Further assessment |
| Transient slowing, associated with probe pressure, in the second trimester | Seen in normal fetuses |
| Stays at 110 per minute or below in a well fetus | Timely specialist evaluation |
| Brief rise to 160 to 180 per minute with movement | Can be a normal variant |
| Stays at 180 per minute or above | Further evaluation |


## Rhythm findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography

The guideline lists these among the fetal indications for fetal echocardiography: persistent tachycardia at 180 beats per minute or more, suspected heart block or persistent bradycardia at 110 or less, and a rhythm that is frequently or persistently irregular. [7]


## How the echocardiography guideline words it

The echocardiography guideline describes a sustained rate below 120 beats per minute as abnormal at any gestation, and a sustained rate above 160 to 180 as abnormal. The screening guideline sets its thresholds for referral at 110 or less and 180 or more. This unit teaches the screening thresholds. [8, 9, 4, 6]


## What the specialist will do

Every fetal echocardiogram must document the heart rate and rhythm. [10]

Repeated blocked premature atrial beats can look like second- or third-degree heart block and must be told apart from it. [11]

When the rhythm is irregular, slow or fast, the mechanism should be documented with M-mode, pulsed-wave Doppler or tissue Doppler, alone or together. [12]

M-mode times the atria against the ventricles: the cursor passes through an atrial wall and the free wall of a ventricle together. [13]

Pulsed-wave Doppler does the same by sampling two flows at once: superior vena cava with ascending aorta, mitral inflow with aortic outflow, or pulmonary artery with pulmonary vein. [14]

Knowing what these techniques are helps you explain to the family why they are being referred.

## Rate and rhythm at every screen

- [ ] Rate between 120 and 160 per minute [1]
- [ ] Rhythm regular [1]
- [ ] Rate stays at 110 or below in a well fetus: timely specialist evaluation arranged [4]
- [ ] Persistent rate of 180 or above: further evaluation arranged [6]
- [ ] Ectopic beats more often than every three to five beats: further assessment arranged [3]
- [ ] Rhythm irregular for more than one to two weeks: further assessment arranged [3]

## Still to be written

- How urgently each rhythm finding should be seen (same day, within a week) - not stated in the screening guideline; needs a source and the editor's decision.
- Signs that a fetus with an arrhythmia is unwell (hydrops, effusions) and what the screener should record - needs a source.
- How to count the fetal heart rate reliably at screening (M-mode or Doppler method) - needs a source.
- What to do with patterns the guideline does not grade (for example a rate between 110 and 120, or occasional ectopic beats at a single visit): a complete triage scheme needs a source or the editor's teaching.
- Maternal conditions linked to heart block and how they change follow-up - planned for XC4.

# The heart at 11 to 14 weeks

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D9 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- State the place of early cardiac screening in low-risk pregnancies: shown to be effective, but not routine or mandatory.
- Give the minimum cardiac check at the early scan.
- List the components of a detailed early cardiac screen.
- Apply the Doppler safety limits for early pregnancy.
- Say which nuchal translucency measurements lead to cardiac referral.

## Where early screening stands

The screening guideline is written for low-risk pregnancies in the second trimester. It also considers screening in the late first and early second trimester where this is technically feasible. [1]

First-trimester cardiac screening has been shown to be effective in low-risk populations. It is neither routine nor mandatory. Where possible, it can be done at the nuchal translucency scan. [2]

The cardiac screening examination is performed optimally between 18 and 22 weeks. [3]


## The minimum

The minimum requirements at an early screen are to see the heart within the chest and to confirm a regular rhythm. [4]

Cardiac structures are seen successfully significantly more often after 12 weeks and 3 days. [4]


## Equipment

High-frequency transabdominal transducers are recommended for early screening; a transvaginal transducer may be used. Colour Doppler, or high-quality power Doppler with bidirectional flow mapping, or both, are used in addition to grey-scale. [5]

The echocardiography guideline notes that frequencies of 5 to 12 MHz may help in the late first and early second trimesters. [6]


## Safety

In early screening, use Doppler mainly for the four-chamber view and the three-vessel-and-trachea view. Keep the thermal index at 1.0 or less. Keep exposure as short as possible, usually no more than 5 to 10 minutes. [7]

For early fetal echocardiography, which is a different examination, the echocardiography guideline says to keep the thermal and mechanical indices at or below 1.0 and to use Doppler sparingly. [8]


## A detailed early cardiac screen

When a detailed early screen is done, three components are recommended. [9]

| Component | Mode | What to show |
|---|---|---|
| Situs and cardiac axis | Grey-scale | Situs and cardiac axis |
| Four-chamber view | Grey-scale, and colour and/or bidirectional power Doppler | The four-chamber view on both |
| Three-vessel-and-trachea view | Colour and/or bidirectional power Doppler | Aortic and ductal arches, both on the left |

Two practical points for the early four-chamber view with colour: a posterior fetal spine is the preferred position for showing inflow into both ventricles, and the balance between colour and grey-scale is adjusted to favour the flow signal in the small structures. [10, 11]


## Limits of the early scan

Outflow-tract views are often difficult in early gestation and are prone to both false-negative and false-positive diagnosis. [12]

Suspicion of congenital heart disease at the early scan should lead to referral for early fetal echocardiography. [12]

Some lesions are not discovered until later in pregnancy. [13]


## What the echocardiography guideline adds

These points come from the guideline on fetal echocardiography, the specialist examination. They are included so the screener knows what happens after an early referral.

Suspicion of a cardiac anomaly in the late first trimester should prompt consideration of an early fetal echocardiogram, depending on available expertise and resources. Evidence is insufficient to recommend fetal echocardiography before 16 weeks for low-risk pregnancies. [14, 15]

Early imaging has limits. Assessment of the pulmonary and systemic veins is limited, and limited resolution can hide subtle defects, including valve lesions. [16, 17]

When early findings are uncertain or suspicious, a repeat examination within 1 to 2 weeks is suggested. Even after a normal detailed early examination, a repeat study is recommended at 18 to 20 weeks. [18, 19]

Early counselling and reporting should mention the possibility of missed diagnoses and of lesions that progress later. [20]


## Nuchal translucency and the heart

A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks is an indication for detailed cardiac evaluation. This holds even if the measurement later falls into the normal range. [21]

With a nuchal translucency of 3.0 to 3.4 mm, fetal echocardiography may be considered. [22]

## Early cardiac screen

- [ ] Minimum: heart within the chest [4]
- [ ] Minimum: rhythm regular [4]
- [ ] If a detailed early screen is done: situs and cardiac axis on grey-scale [9]
- [ ] If a detailed early screen is done: four-chamber view on grey-scale and on colour and/or bidirectional power Doppler [9]
- [ ] If a detailed early screen is done: three-vessel-and-trachea view on colour and/or bidirectional power Doppler, both arches on the left [9]
- [ ] When Doppler is used: thermal index 1.0 or less; exposure kept short [7]
- [ ] Nuchal translucency 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks: detailed cardiac evaluation arranged [21]
- [ ] Suspicion of heart disease: referred for early fetal echocardiography [12]

## Still to be written

- An explicit statement, for screening, that a normal early cardiac scan does not replace the second-trimester screen. The echocardiography guideline says this for early fetal echocardiography (claim AS23-109); the editor to decide whether the course states it for screening (question Q2).
- Other first-trimester markers linked to heart disease (tricuspid regurgitation, ductus venosus flow) - not in the screening guideline; needs a source.
- Which lesions can and cannot be detected at 11 to 14 weeks, with detection rates - needs a source.
- Transvaginal technique for the early heart - needs a source.

# Normal variants, artefacts and pitfalls

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D10 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- Recognise the normal findings that are commonly mistaken for disease.
- Recognise the technical artefact that fakes a septal defect.
- Know which 'variants' are only variants at a certain gestation or for a certain time.

## How to use this unit

Each item below is paired with its limit: the point at which it stops being a variant. A variant without its limit is how abnormal hearts get passed as normal.


## A rim of fluid around the heart

A small amount of pericardial fluid, 2 mm or less thick at end-systole, is common in the second and third trimesters and is normal. A thin dark rim around the heart should not be mistaken for an effusion. [1]


## A gap in the septum that is not there

With the beam running parallel to the ventricular septum, acoustic drop-out can falsely suggest a defect near the crux. The septum is seen best with the beam perpendicular to it. [2]

Real small defects exist too. Defects of 1 to 2 mm can be very difficult to confirm, particularly when fetal size and position are unfavourable; most are of limited clinical significance and may close before birth. [3, 4]


## Ventricles that are not quite equal

Mild disproportion between the ventricles can be a normal variant in the third trimester. [5]

The limit: right-left asymmetry in mid-gestation warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return. [5]


## Great arteries that are not quite equal

The pulmonary artery is usually slightly larger than the ascending aorta in fetal life. [6]

The limit: the great arteries should be approximately equal, and a major discrepancy should lead to further evaluation. [7]


## A skipped beat

Ectopic beats are the most common rhythm disturbance. They are often benign and resolve on their own, and in low-risk populations they are not associated with a higher risk of structural heart disease. [8]

The limit: episodes more often than every three to five beats, or a rhythm that stays irregular for more than one to two weeks, are an indication for further assessment. [9]


## A brief slow or fast rate

Transient bradycardia, associated with transducer pressure, is seen in normal second-trimester fetuses. Mild transient tachycardia of 160 to 180 beats per minute can be a normal variant during fetal movement. [10, 11]

The limit: a rate that stays at 110 or below in a well fetus needs timely specialist evaluation, and a rate that stays at 180 or above should be evaluated further. [10, 11]


## A bright spot in a ventricle

For an echogenic intracardiac focus, the guideline finds insufficient evidence that the risk of congenital heart disease is significantly above baseline. [12]


## Two arches that will not sit in one picture

The aortic arch lies slightly nearer the head than the ductal arch. Showing both together may need a small adjustment away from a true axial plane; failing to see both in one strict axial cut is not in itself abnormal. [13]


## A dark area in front of the great vessels

On the upper mediastinal views the thymus appears as a relatively dark area between the great vessels and the front of the chest. [14]


## A poor view is not a normal view

When the fetal lie is unfavourable, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed. [15]

Cardiac axis and position can still be judged when the four-chamber view itself is not seen well. [16]

## Before calling it abnormal, and before calling it a variant

- [ ] Fluid rim: 2 mm or less at end-systole is normal [1]
- [ ] Septal gap near the crux: re-examined with the beam perpendicular [2]
- [ ] Ventricular asymmetry: gestation checked (mid-gestation needs further examination) [5]
- [ ] Great arteries: slight difference is usual; major discrepancy needs further evaluation [6, 7]
- [ ] Ectopic beats: frequency and duration checked against the limits [9]
- [ ] Slow or fast rate: transient or persistent [10, 11]

## Still to be written

- Echogenic intracardiac focus: appearance, where it lies, and how to tell it from other bright structures - needs a source.
- Other variants and look-alikes not named in the guideline: prominent moderator band, redundant foramen ovale flap, prominent coronary sinus, trivial tricuspid regurgitation, linear insertion of the valves - each needs a source.
- Artefacts beyond septal drop-out: shadowing from ribs and spine, reverberation, colour bleeding - planned with XA4; needs a physics source.
- The editor's own list of pitfalls from 14 years of practice, with example clips from the archive - this would make the unit distinctive.

# When and how to refer

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D11 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.2

## You will be able to

- Apply the basic rule: a fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography.
- List the fetal findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography.
- List the maternal and family factors that are indications.
- Tell apart factors where echocardiography may be considered and factors with insufficient evidence.
- Say who should perform the fetal echocardiogram and what counselling should take into account.

## The basic rule

A fetus with a known or suspected abnormality on cardiac screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography. [1]

The echocardiography guideline says the same from its side: fetal echocardiography is indicated when the screening ultrasound of the heart is abnormal, whether or not there are other risk factors. [2]

A low threshold for referral is one of the measures that can improve a screening programme. [3]

You do not need to name the lesion: suspicion on an adequate view is enough. A view that could not be obtained is a different situation. With an unfavourable fetal lie, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed. [1, 4]


## Risk factors add to screening; they do not replace it

When there is a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease, fetal echocardiography is indicated in addition to routine screening, depending on local resources, the setting, the availability of examiners and the screening results. [5]

A high proportion of detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor and no extracardiac anomaly. This is why quality screening and timely referral matter. [6]


## Fetal indications

The guideline lists these fetal factors as common indications for fetal echocardiography. [7, 8]

| Fetal factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Suspected structural anomaly of the heart |  |
| Extracardiac structural anomaly | With a known association with congenital heart disease |
| Suspected abnormal function or a large heart |  |
| Hydrops |  |
| Persistent tachycardia | 180 beats per minute or more |
| Suspected heart block |  |
| Persistent bradycardia | 110 beats per minute or less |
| Irregular rhythm | Frequent or persistent |
| Increased nuchal translucency | 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks |
| Genetic abnormality | Confirmed or suspected |
| Monochorionic twins | If resources allow |

A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks remains an indication even if the measurement later becomes normal. [8]


## Findings on the screen that should not be passed

Right-left asymmetry of the ventricles in mid-gestation warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return. [9]

A major difference in size between the two great arteries should lead to further evaluation. [10]

An abnormal cardiac axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly. [11]

If the heart or the stomach is not on the left, suspect a situs abnormality. [12]


## Maternal and family indications

The guideline lists these maternal, family and exposure factors as common indications. [13]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative of the fetus | Parents, siblings and half-siblings |
| Mendelian disease with childhood cardiac manifestations | In a first- or second-degree relative |
| Pregestational diabetes | Whatever the HbA1c |
| Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies |  |
| Phenylketonuria | Unknown status, or periconceptional phenylalanine above 10 mg/dL |
| Retinoid exposure |  |
| Confirmed fetal infection | TORCH or parvovirus B19 |


## May be considered

For some factors the guideline says fetal echocardiography may be considered. [14]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Congenital heart disease in a second-degree relative |  |
| Gestational diabetes | Diagnosed in the first or early second trimester |
| Nuchal translucency | 3.0 to 3.4 mm |
| Selected teratogens | For example paroxetine, carbamazepine, lithium, sodium valproate |
| Conception by IVF | Including ICSI |
| ACE inhibitor use |  |


## Not enough evidence of raised risk

For each of these factors, taken on its own, the guideline finds insufficient evidence that the risk of congenital heart disease is significantly above baseline. [15]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Obesity | BMI 35 kg/m2 or more |
| SSRI exposure | Other than paroxetine |
| Non-cardiac soft markers | For aneuploidy |
| Abnormal serum analytes |  |
| Single umbilical artery | Isolated |
| Gestational diabetes | Diagnosed after the second trimester |
| Warfarin or alcohol exposure |  |
| Echogenic intracardiac focus |  |
| Prenatal fever, or viral infection with seroconversion only |  |
| Congenital heart disease in a distant relative | Isolated; more distant than second degree |

This is a statement about the factor alone. A suspected abnormality on the screen makes the fetus a candidate for fetal echocardiography whatever the history, and a significant risk factor that is also present still counts. [1, 5]

These pregnancies have the same routine cardiac screen as every other: situs, four-chamber view, outflow tracts and great-vessel views. [16]


## How the echocardiography guideline compares

The American echocardiography guideline has its own table of indications. Most entries agree with the screening guideline. The points below are where its wording adds something.

It lists as indications: pregestational diabetes, maternal SSA/SSB antibodies, congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative, hydrops, an extracardiac anomaly, monochorionic twins, and a nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more. [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23]

After IVF, or with a nuchal translucency of 3.0 to 3.4 mm, it says fetal echocardiography may be considered, and that after a normal cardiac screen the decision should take the accuracy of local screening into account. [24, 25]

An isolated single umbilical artery does not by itself indicate fetal echocardiography when the second-trimester cardiac screen is normal. [26]


## Who does the echocardiogram, and what families need

Fetal echocardiography is best performed by a trained specialist who is familiar with prenatal diagnosis and with the course, management and prognosis after birth. [27]

Counselling after a heart problem is detected should take into account the high prevalence of psychological distress in the mother. [27]

Findings on the three-vessel views can change what happens next: testing for 22q11 microdeletion, the planned place of delivery as in complete transposition, readiness to give prostaglandin, or readiness for airway problems from vascular compression. [28]

## Before you close the report: common reasons to refer (not a complete list)

- [ ] Suspected cardiac abnormality on any plane. (A view that could not be obtained is an incomplete scan: more time or a second examination.) [1, 4]
- [ ] Rate stays at 110 or below, or at 180 or above; suspected heart block; frequent or persistently irregular rhythm [7]
- [ ] Ventricles asymmetric in mid-gestation: further examination. Major difference in size between the great arteries: further evaluation [9, 10]
- [ ] Heart or stomach not on the left: suspect a situs abnormality. Abnormal axis: raised risk of a cardiac malformation [12, 11]
- [ ] Extracardiac structural anomaly known to go with heart disease; hydrops; confirmed or suspected genetic abnormality; monochorionic twins if resources allow [7]
- [ ] Nuchal translucency was 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks, even if it later became normal [8]
- [ ] Maternal or family indication: check the full table in this unit (examples: congenital heart disease in a parent, sibling or half-sibling; pregestational diabetes; anti-Ro/SSA antibodies) [13]

## Still to be written

- What a referral letter should contain (views obtained, what failed, gestation, stored clips) - needs a source or the editor's template.
- How urgently each kind of finding should be seen - not in the screening guideline; needs a source and the editor's decision.
- Indian referral pathways, and timing in relation to the legal limits for termination of pregnancy - needs an Indian source and the editor's input.
- What to tell the parents at the moment of referral - unit D12.

Unit D13 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.1

## You will be able to

- Name the four things by which the quality of a screening examination is judged.
- Say what should be stored from every cardiac screen, and why.
- Set up a simple audit of your own images and detection.
- Use a checklist for the five planes on every patient.

## What quality means

The quality of a screening examination is judged on four things: image quality, acquisition of the standard planes, appropriate interpretation of the views, and complete documentation. [1]

The 2023 guideline added sections on quality assurance and on the use of a checklist. [2]


## Why it matters

In one retrospective study of missed diagnoses, failure to meet technical criteria contributed to about half of the misses. Failure to recognise abnormal anatomy on an adequate view accounted for nearly a third more. [3]


## Image quality starts with set-up

Use settings that favour a high frame rate with more contrast and high resolution: low persistence, a single focal zone and a fairly narrow image field. Cardiac presets usually include these. [4]

Magnify until the heart fills at least a third to a half of the screen. [5]


## What to store

Still frames and video clips of the recommended structures and views should be archived, so that the examination can be reviewed later for adequacy. Identify the patient appropriately in the clinical record, label laterality and orientation where appropriate, and take local or national archiving standards into account. [6]

The views of the right ventricular outflow tract, the branch pulmonary arteries and the two arches form a continuum. They are likely to be judged more reliably live or on a clip than from still images alone. [7]

For a full fetal echocardiogram, the echocardiography guideline asks for stills, moving clips and a structured report. It requires a sweep from the stomach to the upper mediastinum, and two-dimensional and colour clips of the individual views, including the three-vessel view and the three-vessel-and-trachea view. [8]

The same guideline says images should be kept in a secure digital archive that allows retrieval for review, that local legal requirements decide how long they are kept, and that a study which stays non-diagnostic after optimisation should have its limitations stated in the report. [9, 10, 11]


## Auditing yourself

Audit of stored stills or clips against quality criteria set in advance is encouraged. [12]

Each practice is encouraged to review its own detection rates and diagnostic accuracy every year, and to arrange further training where the review shows a need. [12]

Continuous training based on feedback, standardised protocols, a low threshold for referral and easy access to fetal heart specialists can all improve a programme. For fetal echocardiography services, ongoing quality improvement should be documented. [13, 14]

How a practice samples its studies and scores them is a local decision. The guideline gives no method, and none is taught here; see the missing claims for this unit.


## The checklist

The checklist below gathers the main criteria for the five planes, for learning and for audit. It is a selection. Completing it does not by itself establish a complete normal examination.

## Five-plane screening checklist (main criteria)

- [ ] Fetal left and right worked out first [15]
- [ ] Upper abdomen at the abdominal circumference level: stomach on the left; descending aorta left of the spine; inferior vena cava right of the spine [16]
- [ ] Heart mainly in the left chest; usually no larger than a third of the chest area [17, 18]
- [ ] Axis about 45 degrees to the left (plus or minus 20) of the front-to-back axis of the chest [18]
- [ ] Rate 120 to 160 per minute, regular [19]
- [ ] Atria similar in size; foramen ovale flap moving within the left atrium; septum primum present [20]
- [ ] At least one pulmonary vein seen entering the left atrium on grey-scale, where technically feasible [21]
- [ ] Ventricles similar in size, walls not thick; moderator band near the apex marks the right ventricle. Asymmetry in mid-gestation needs further examination; mild disproportion can be a third-trimester variant [22, 23]
- [ ] Ventricular septum examined from apex to crux, with the adequacy of the view recorded [24, 25]
- [ ] Two atrioventricular valves opening separately and freely; septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve inserted nearer the apex [26]
- [ ] LVOT: vessel from the left ventricle, anterior wall continuous with the septum, not dividing; valve not thickened, moving freely [27, 28, 29]
- [ ] RVOT: vessel from the right ventricle, dividing after a short course; valve not thickened, moving freely [27, 30]
- [ ] Great arteries cross and are approximately equal in size [31, 27]
- [ ] Three-vessel view: number, size, alignment and arrangement of the three vessels [32]
- [ ] Three-vessel-and-trachea view: V shape, both arches left of the trachea, arches similar in size [33, 34]
- [ ] Stills and clips of the recommended views stored; laterality and orientation labelled where appropriate [6]

## Still to be written

- A scoring system for image quality of each cardiac plane (published criteria with points) - needs a source.
- A target or benchmark detection rate to audit against - needs a source; none is stated in the guideline claims held.
- How long images must be kept and how PC-PNDT record-keeping applies to stored clips in India - the echocardiography guideline only says to follow local legal requirements (AS23-114); needs an Indian legal source and the advisor's input.
- A method for sampling studies, scoring them and working out a practice's own detection rate and accuracy - not given in the guideline; needs a source or the editor's design.
- How to obtain outcome feedback after delivery in Indian practice - needs the editor's input.
